results.title: Ones-diagonal determinant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$, the determinant $A_k(p_1, \dots, p_k)$ is the determinant of the $k \times k$ integer matrix with $p_1, \dots, p_k$ on the diagonal and $1$ in every other entry.

results.title: Bordered ones-diagonal matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$, the $(k+1) \times (k+1)$ integer matrix whose first row consists of ones and whose row $i + 1$, for $1 \le i \le k$, has $p_i$ in column $i$ and $1$ in every other column. Equivalently, it is the $k \times k$ matrix with diagonal entries $p_1, \dots, p_k$ and all other entries $1$, with a column of ones appended on the right and then a row of ones placed on top.

results.title: Bordered ones-diagonal determinant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$, the integer $F_k(p_1, \dots, p_k)$ is $(-1)^k$ times the determinant of the bordered ones-diagonal matrix of $p_1, \dots, p_k$: the $(k+1) \times (k+1)$ integer matrix whose first row consists of ones and whose row $i + 1$, for $1 \le i \le k$, has $p_i$ in column $i$ and $1$ in every other column.

results.title: The first primes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $k$, the $k$-tuple whose entry with index $i$, for $0 \le i < k$, is the $(i+1)$-st prime; that is, the first $k$ primes $2, 3, 5, \dots$ in increasing order.

results.title: Residue hit count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$, $r_1, \dots, r_k$ and $n$, the residue hit count $\gamma(n)$ is the number of indices $i$ with $n \equiv r_i \pmod{p_i}$, that is, the number of the residue classes $r_i \bmod p_i$ that contain $n$.

results.title: Number of available integers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$ and $r_1, \dots, r_k$, let $\gamma(n)$ be the number of indices $i$ with $n \equiv r_i \pmod{p_i}$, and call $n$ available if $\gamma(n) \le 1$. This is the number of available integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k$. For the first $k$ primes it is the count written $\mathrm{av}(k)$.

results.title: Free count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$ and $r_1, \dots, r_k$, let $\gamma(n)$ be the number of indices $i$ with $n \equiv r_i \pmod{p_i}$. The free count is the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le p_1 \cdots p_k$ and $\gamma(n) = 0$.

results.title: Occupied count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $p_1, \dots, p_k$ and $r_1, \dots, r_k$, let $\gamma(n)$ be the number of indices $i$ with $n \equiv r_i \pmod{p_i}$. The occupied count is the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le p_1 \cdots p_k$ and $\gamma(n) > 1$.

results.title: Recurrence for the bordered determinants of the first primes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k \ge 2$ and let $p_1, \dots, p_k$ be the first $k$ primes. For $m \le k$ let $f_m = F_m(p_1, \dots, p_m)$, where $F_m(p_1, \dots, p_m)$ is $(-1)^m$ times the determinant of the $(m+1) \times (m+1)$ matrix whose first row consists of ones and whose row $i + 1$, for $1 \le i \le m$, has $p_i$ in column $i$ and $1$ in every other column. Then $f_k = (p_k - 1) f_{k-1}$.

results.title: Lemma 3, free recurrence
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Covering dimension at most n
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A topological space $X$ has covering dimension at most $n \in \mathbb{N}$ if every finite open cover $U_1, \dots, U_m$ of $X$ has a finite open refinement $V_1, \dots, V_k$ (open sets covering $X$, each contained in some $U_i$) in which any $n + 2$ members with distinct indices have empty intersection, that is, the refinement has order at most $n + 1$.

results.title: Small inductive and covering dimension can differ for compact Hausdorff spaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Scottish Book Problem 187, part (2), has a negative answer: it is not the case that for every compact Hausdorff space $X$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X$ has small inductive dimension at most $n$ if and only if $X$ has covering dimension at most $n$.

results.title: Scottish Book Problem 167
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Ulam's claim that for every infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space $H$ with unit sphere $S = \{p \in H : \|p\| = 1\}$, every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all continuous functions $f_1, \dots, f_n : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and every continuous map $T : S \to S$, there is a point $p_0 \in S$ with $f_i(T(p_0)) = f_i(p_0)$ for every $i$.

results.title: Negative answer to Scottish Book Problem 167
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Ulam's claim in Problem 167 is false: there are an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space $H$ with unit sphere $S$, a number $n \in \mathbb{N}$, continuous functions $f_1, \dots, f_n : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and a continuous map $T : S \to S$ such that no point $p_0 \in S$ satisfies $f_i(T(p_0)) = f_i(p_0)$ for every $i$.

results.title: Projective Hilbert space
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed additive commutative group, in practice a real inner product space. The projective Hilbert space of $E$ is the quotient of the unit sphere $\{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ by the relation identifying each $x$ with $-x$. Its points are the antipodal pairs $\{x, -x\}$ of unit vectors, that is, the diameters of the unit sphere.

results.title: Projective Hilbert space homeomorphic to the space itself
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real inner product space $E$, the statement that the projective Hilbert space of $E$, the unit sphere $\{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ with each $x$ identified with $-x$ and given the quotient topology, is homeomorphic to $E$.

results.title: Projective Hilbert space is not homeomorphic to Hilbert space
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Then the projective Hilbert space of $E$, the unit sphere $\{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ with each $x$ identified with $-x$ and given the quotient topology, is not homeomorphic to $E$.

results.title: Retraction onto the unit sphere of Hilbert space
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space and let $S = \{x \in E : \|x\| = 1\}$ be its unit sphere. Then there is a continuous map $f : E \to E$ such that $f(x) \in S$ for every $x \in E$ and $f(x) = x$ for every $x \in S$.

results.title: Scottish Book Problem 7 (Mazur–Banach)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The claim that in every real Banach space $E$, any two closed convex subsets $A, B \subseteq E$ whose linear spans are infinite-dimensional are homeomorphic, with the subspace topologies.

results.title: Scottish Book Problem 7 fails: closed convex sets need not be homeomorphic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Scottish Book Problem 7 claim is false: there are a real Banach space $E$ and closed convex subsets $A, B \subseteq E$, each with infinite-dimensional linear span, that are not homeomorphic.

results.title: Integrability of the scaled gamma integrand
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For real numbers $a > 0$ and $s > 0$, the function $x \mapsto x^{a-1} e^{-sx}$ is Lebesgue integrable on the open half-line $(0, \infty)$.

results.title: Exponential moments of the gamma distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a > 0$ and $r > 0$. For every real $t < r$, the function $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ is integrable with respect to the gamma distribution with shape $a$ and rate $r$.

results.title: Moment generating function of the gamma distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a > 0$ and $r > 0$, and let $X$ have the gamma distribution with shape $a$ and rate $r$. For every real $t < r$, the moment generating function of $X$ at $t$ is $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \left(\frac{r}{r - t}\right)^a$.

results.title: Half-line of exponential integrability for the gamma distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a > 0$ and $r > 0$, and let $S$ be the set of real $t$ such that $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ is integrable with respect to the gamma distribution with shape $a$ and rate $r$. Then the half-line $(-\infty, r)$ is contained in $S$.

results.title: A neighbourhood of zero of exponential integrability for the gamma distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a > 0$, $r > 0$ and $0 < \varepsilon < r$, and let $S$ be the set of real $t$ such that $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ is integrable with respect to the gamma distribution with shape $a$ and rate $r$. Then the interval $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ is contained in the interior of $S$.

results.title: Real moments of the gamma law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Real moments of the gamma law: for shape `a > 0`, rate `r > 0` and `p > -a`, `E[X ^ p] = Γ(a + p) / (Γ(a) r ^ p)`. (The law is carried by `[0, ∞)`, so the values of `x ^ p` for `x < 0` play no role.)

results.title: Mean of the gamma law

results.title: Scaling a gamma random variable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Scaling a gamma variable by `c > 0` keeps its shape and divides its rate by `c`: `c X ~ Gamma(a, r / c)` when `X ~ Gamma(a, r)`.

results.title: Upper tail of the gamma law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The upper tail of the gamma law: `P(X > c) = Γ(a, r c) / Γ(a)` for `c ≥ 0`.

results.title: Erlang tail formula

results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An encoded context-free grammar over a terminal type $T$ consists of a start nonterminal, which is a natural number, and a list of productions. Each production is a pair of a left-hand side, a natural number, and a right-hand side, a list of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$, in which a number $i$ from the left summand stands for nonterminal $i$ and an element $a$ of $T$ for terminal $a$.

results.title: Decoding a grammar symbol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Decoding sends an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$ to a grammar symbol with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$: a natural number $i$ from the left summand goes to the nonterminal $i$, and an element $a$ of $T$ from the right summand goes to the terminal $a$.

results.title: Encoding a grammar symbol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Encoding sends a grammar symbol with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$ to an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$: the terminal $a$ goes to $a$ in the right summand $T$, and the nonterminal $i$ goes to $i$ in the left summand $\mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Decoding a production
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Decoding a pair $(A, s)$ of a natural number $A$ and a list $s$ of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$ gives the production, with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$, whose left-hand side is the nonterminal $A$ and whose right-hand side is $s$ with each entry decoded as a symbol: a number $i$ from the left summand becomes the nonterminal $i$ and an element $a$ of $T$ becomes the terminal $a$.

results.title: Encoding a production
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Encoding a production with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$ gives the pair $(A, s)$ where $A \in \mathbb{N}$ is its left-hand side and $s$ is its right-hand side with each symbol encoded as an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$: the terminal $a$ becomes $a$ in the right summand and the nonterminal $i$ becomes $i$ in the left summand.

results.title: Grammar denoted by an encoding
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$, the context-free grammar over $T$ whose nonterminals are the natural numbers, whose initial nonterminal is the start nonterminal of $g$, and whose productions are the decodings of the encoded productions of $g$: an encoded production $(i, u)$ becomes the production rewriting the nonterminal $i$ to the word obtained from $u$ by reading each entry $\mathrm{inl}\, j$…

results.title: Language of an encoded grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The language of an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ is the language generated by the context-free grammar that $g$ denotes, whose nonterminals are the natural numbers, whose initial nonterminal is the start nonterminal of $g$ and whose productions are the decoded productions of $g$.

results.title: Encoded grammars generate context-free languages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The language of an encoded grammar is context-free.

results.title: Nonterminal of a symbol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The partial map from grammar symbols with terminals in $T$ and nonterminals in $N$ to $N$ that sends a nonterminal $A$ to $A$ and has no value on terminals.

results.title: List of nonterminals mentioned by a grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$, the list consisting of the initial nonterminal of $G$ followed, for each production of $G$ in turn (in some fixed order of its finite set of productions), by the left-hand side of the production and then the nonterminals of its right-hand side in order. Nonterminals may occur more than once.

results.title: Numbering of nonterminals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$, the number of a nonterminal $A$ of $G$ is the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first); if $A$ does not occur in that list, its number is the length of the list.

results.title: Nonterminal with a given number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$ and a natural number $n$, the nonterminal of $G$ with number $n$ is the entry at position $n$, counting from $0$, of the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first); if the list has no entry at position $n$, it is the initial nonterminal of $G$.

results.title: Numbering the nonterminals of a production and back recovers it
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a context-free grammar over $T$ and $r$ a production of $G$. Replacing each nonterminal $A$ of $r$ by its number, the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions, and then replacing each number $n$ by the nonterminal of $G$ with number $n$ (the entry at position $n$ of that list, or the initial nonterminal of $G$ if the list has no such entry)…

results.title: Encoding of a context-free grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a context-free grammar $G$ over $T$, the encoded grammar whose start nonterminal is the number of the initial nonterminal of $G$ and whose productions are the productions of $G$, listed in some fixed order, with every nonterminal $A$ replaced by its number, the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first).

results.title: The encoding of a grammar generates the same language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The encoding of a grammar generates the same language.

results.title: A language is context-free exactly when an encoded grammar generates it
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A language is context-free exactly when an encoded grammar generates it.

results.title: Encoded grammars as pairs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Sending an encoded grammar over $T$ to the pair of its start nonterminal and its list of productions is a bijection from encoded grammars over $T$ onto pairs $(s, R)$ of a natural number $s$ and a list $R$ of pairs of a natural number and a list of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$.

results.title: Result of breadth-first search
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A breadth-first search result on a vertex type $V$ consists of a distance function, assigning to each vertex either a natural number or none, and a list of vertices. They are meant to record the shortest distance from the source (none when the vertex is unreachable) and the vertices in first-discovery order.

results.title: List model of breadth-first search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and a source vertex $s$, the list model keeps a list of processed pairs and a queue of pairs $(v, d)$ of a vertex and a distance, starting with no processed pairs and the queue $[(s, 0)]$. It performs one round per vertex of $G$: if the queue is empty, nothing changes; otherwise the front pair $(u, d)$ is removed from the queue and recorded as…

results.title: Breadth-first search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and a source vertex $s$, breadth-first search keeps a FIFO queue of pairs $(v, d)$ of a vertex and a distance and a table of discovered vertices with their distances, starting with the queue $[(s, 0)]$ and $s$ discovered at distance $0$. It performs one round per vertex of $G$: if the queue is empty, nothing changes; otherwise it dequeues the front pair…

results.title: The executable BFS agrees with the list model
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every source vertex $s$, the result of the executable breadth-first search from $s$ equals the result of the list model of breadth-first search from $s$: both report the same distance (or none) for every vertex and the same first-discovery order.

results.title: Breadth-first search on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a natural number $n$, an adjacency function assigning to each vertex $i < n$ an ordered list of vertices among $0, \dots, n-1$, and a source vertex $s < n$, this is the result of breadth-first search from $s$ on the finite directed graph with vertex enumeration $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ and these adjacency lists.

reading_title.source: Breadth-first search on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$

results.title: BFS reports a distance exactly for the reachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and all vertices $s$ and $v$, breadth-first search from $s$ reports some distance for $v$ (rather than none) if and only if $v$ is reachable from $s$ in $G$.

results.title: BFS lists exactly the reachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and all vertices $s$ and $v$, the vertex $v$ occurs in the first-discovery order of breadth-first search from $s$ if and only if $v$ is reachable from $s$ in $G$.

results.title: BFS discovers each vertex at most once
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$, no vertex occurs twice in the first-discovery order of breadth-first search from $s$.

results.title: BFS reports exactly the shortest walk length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists, all vertices $s$ and $v$, and every natural number $d$, breadth-first search from $s$ reports distance $d$ for $v$ if and only if there is a walk of exactly $d$ edges from $s$ to $v$ in $G$ and $d \le k$ for every natural number $k$ such that there is a walk of exactly $k$ edges from $s$ to $v$.

results.title: Breadth-first search places the source at distance zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$ of $G$, breadth-first search in $G$ from $s$ reports a distance for $s$ itself, and that distance is $0$ edges.

results.title: BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$, the distances reported by breadth-first search from $s$, listed along its first-discovery order, form a nondecreasing sequence, where a vertex without a reported distance counts as $0$.

results.title: Breadth-first search forest
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A breadth-first search forest on a vertex type $V$ consists of a breadth-first search result, namely a partial distance function from $V$ to the natural numbers and a list of vertices, together with a partial predecessor function from $V$ to $V$. For a search from a source vertex $s$, these are meant to give the distance from $s$ of each reachable vertex, the reachable vertices in first-discovery order, and the…

results.title: Breadth-first search with parent pointers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a finite directed graph $G$ on a vertex type $V$, with ordered adjacency lists, and a source vertex $s$, this runs first-in-first-out breadth-first search from $s$ for $|V|$ rounds. The queue starts with $s$ at distance $0$. Each round tries to dequeue a vertex $u$; if it succeeds, it scans the neighbors of $u$ in adjacency-list order, and each neighbor not yet discovered gets distance one more than $u$,…

results.title: Path reconstruction from BFS parents
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be the predecessor function of a breadth-first search forest, let $n$ be the length of its discovery order, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. Starting from $v_k = t$, this walks back along $p$, setting $v_{i-1} = p(v_i)$, until it reaches a vertex $v_0$ that tests equal to $s$, and returns the list $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$. It returns no list if the walk meets a vertex that does not test equal to $s$ and has…

results.title: Breadth-first search with parents returns the ordinary BFS result
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every source vertex $s$, the output of breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$, with its cost and its predecessor table forgotten, equals the result of ordinary FIFO breadth-first search from $s$ in $G$: the same distance table and the same first-discovery order.

results.title: Exactly the source and the unreachable vertices have no BFS parent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. A vertex $v$ has no recorded predecessor in $F$ if and only if $v = s$ or $v$ is not reachable from $s$ along directed edges of $G$.

results.title: BFS parents are joined by graph edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. If $F$ records $p$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then $G$ has a directed edge from $p$ to $v$, that is, $v$ occurs in the adjacency list of $p$.

results.title: A BFS parent is one step closer to the source
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. If $F$ records $p$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then there is a natural number $d$ such that $F$ records distance $d$ for $p$ and distance $d + 1$ for $v$.

results.title: The BFS parent is the first discovered in-neighbour
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. For every vertex $v \ne s$, the predecessor that $F$ records for $v$ is the first vertex $u$, in the first-discovery order of ordinary FIFO breadth-first search from $s$ in $G$, whose adjacency list contains $v$; if no vertex in that order has…

results.title: Each reachable vertex has a unique saved-parent chain
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices with $v$ reachable from $s$ in $G$. There is exactly one list of vertices that starts at $s$, ends at $v$, and in which each vertex after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent in the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$.

results.title: Saved-parent chains are simple
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. If a list of vertices starts at $s$, ends at $v$, and each of its vertices after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent in the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$, then no vertex occurs twice in the list.

results.title: The saved-parent relation is acyclic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. In the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$, there is no sequence $v = x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k = v$ with $k \ge 1$ in which each $x_i$ is the saved parent of $x_{i+1}$.

results.title: Path reconstruction at the source
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every breadth-first search forest $F$ and every vertex $s$, following the saved parents of $F$ from $s$ back to $s$ returns the one-vertex path $[s]$. This holds for every forest, including one whose discovery order is empty.

results.title: Path reconstruction fails exactly at unreachable vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ towards $s$ returns no path if and only if $v$ is not reachable from $s$ in $G$.

results.title: Reconstructed BFS paths are shortest paths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, let $s$ and $v$ be vertices, and suppose that following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ returns a list $P$ of vertices. Then $P$ starts at $s$ and ends at $v$, each vertex of $P$ after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent, $G$ has an edge from each vertex of $P$ to the next, no vertex…

results.title: Cost of path reconstruction for a reachable vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, let $s$ and $v$ be vertices, and suppose breadth-first search from $s$ reports distance $d$ for $v$. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ costs exactly $3d + 2$, counting one unit for each comparison with $s$, each parent lookup and each vertex prepended to the path.

results.title: Cost of path reconstruction for an unreachable vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices with $v$ not reachable from $s$ in $G$. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ costs exactly $2$, counting one unit for each comparison with $s$, each parent lookup and each vertex prepended to the path: one comparison of $v$ with $s$ and one lookup of the missing parent…

results.title: Exact cost of BFS with parents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with vertex list $V$ and adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}(u)$, let $s$ be a vertex, and let $L$ be the list of vertices in the order in which breadth-first search from $s$ discovers them. The cost of breadth-first search with parents from $s$, counting dequeue attempts, adjacency checks, enqueues and parent writes, equals $|V| + \sum_{u \in L} |\mathrm{adj}(u)| + |L| + (|L| - 1)$,…

results.title: Linear bound on the cost of BFS with parents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with vertex list $V$ and adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}(u)$, and let $s$ be a vertex. The cost of breadth-first search with parents from $s$, counting dequeue attempts, adjacency checks, enqueues and parent writes, is at most $3|V| + \sum_{u \in V} |\mathrm{adj}(u)|$, where adjacency lists are counted with repetitions.

results.title: The k-mers of a string
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The `k`-mers of `s` in order of position: the length-`k` windows `(s.drop i).take k` for `i + k ≤ |s|`.

results.title: Efficient executable computation of k-mers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Executable form of `kmers`: the suffixes of `s` are generated once by `List.tails`, so the cost is `O(|s| · k)` rather than the `Θ(|s|²)` of recomputing `s.drop i` for every `i`. The compiler uses it in place of `kmers` (`kmers_eq_kmersImpl`).

results.title: De Bruijn edge of a k-mer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The edge of the de Bruijn multigraph contributed by a `k`-mer `w`: from its prefix `(k-1)`-mer `w.dropLast` to its suffix `(k-1)`-mer `w.tail`.

results.title: De Bruijn multigraph of a string
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The de Bruijn multigraph of `s` (Pevzner–Tang–Waterman 2001) as its list of edge occurrences: one edge per `k`-mer occurrence, in order of position.

results.title: String spelled by a walk of (k-1)-mers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The string spelled by a walk of `(k-1)`-mers: the first vertex followed by the last letter of each later vertex.

results.title: The `(k-1)`-mer walk of `s` traverses the de Bruijn multigraph in order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Its steps are exactly the edges contributed by the `k`-mers of `s`, one per occurrence, in order of position.

results.title: The `k`-mer walk of `s` is an Eulerian trail
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The `k`-mer walk of `s` is an Eulerian trail of its de Bruijn multigraph: its steps are a permutation of the edge occurrences, each traversed once.

results.title: The (k-1)-mer walk of a string spells the string
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The `(k-1)`-mer walk of `s` spells `s` back (`2 ≤ k`, `k - 1 ≤ |s|`).

results.title: Every Eulerian trail spells a string with the same `k`-mer multiset
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every Eulerian trail spells a string with the same `k`-mer multiset (`2 ≤ k`): if `W` is a walk of `(k-1)`-mers whose steps are a permutation of the edge occurrences of the de Bruijn multigraph of `s`, then the `k`-mers of the spelled string are a permutation of those of `s`. (The empty walk is allowed: it is a trail only when `s` has no `k`-mers, and spells `[]`.)
